Kailash OS keeps the distribution contract that made Kali Linux the default
security environment: curated tooling, category navigation, live images, and
self-consistent surfaces. The AI systems stack is the surface Kali Linux never
mapped. Kailash OS applies the same contract to this stack. The Nix flakes
define everything that attacks, defends, or runs an AI system exactly once.

## The four pillars

Kailash targets four domains. Each pillar ships twice: offensive tooling in the
ATTACK layer; build-side or defensive tooling in the DEFENCE and OPS layers:

- **AppSec** — classic application security assessment (CLASSIC layer, software only)
- **APISec** — web, API, and AI-endpoint runtime assessment
- **MLSec** — adversarial ML: evasion, poisoning, extraction, and inference attacks (predictive AI)
- **AISec** — LLM, agentic, and MCP security: prompt injection, tool-use attacks, supply chain

## Taxonomy

The tool set carries a **CORE substrate plus four named tool layers**. The
taxonomy holds 32 census categories: 31 shippable categories + 1 opt-in data
pack. CORE —
kernel, base userland, hardening, safety defaults, desktop, CLI and menu
engines — hosts no tool categories; every image inherits it. The generated
[Tools page](tools.html) carries the slot census at the current pin.

| Layer | Ids | Purpose | Categories |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CORE** | — | system substrate, no tool categories | kernel, hardening, safety defaults, desktop(s), CLI/menu engines |
| **CLASSIC** | C-1…C-10 | traditional software security assessment (Kali heritage) | Information Gathering · Vulnerability Analysis · Web App Assessment · Database Assessment · Password & Offline-Credential · Reverse Engineering · Signal & SDR (opt-in) · Exploitation & Post-Exploitation · Forensics/IR · Runtime AppSec for AI |
| **ATTACK** | A-1…A-8 | AI offensive tooling, MITRE ATLAS-mapped | AI Recon · LLM Prompt Injection & Jailbreaking · Agentic/MCP & Tool-Use · Model Supply Chain · Model Extraction/Inversion · Multi-modal · AI System Exploitation · Data Poisoning |
| **DEFENCE** | D-1…D-7 | AI defensive and assurance tooling | Runtime Defence & Guardrails · Detection & Observability · Evals & Benchmarks · Provenance & Signing · Threat Modelling · Governance Mapping · Standards Verification |
| **OPS** | O-1…O-7 | the platform the other layers attack and defend | MLOps · Compute & Serving · Vector Stores · Local LLM · SDKs & Dev Env · Docs & Authoring · Agent & MCP Operability |

One manifest generates the navigation. Three views mirror the
practitioner's three questions: **layer-first** (the menu), **tactic-first**
(the MITRE ATLAS matrix), and **standard-first** (the ASVS / AISVS / MLSVS /
OWASP LLM Top 10 evidence views).

## Architecture

Two repositories and a website mirror the nixpkgs↔NixOS split:

- `kailash-packages` — the overlay: every bespoke tool derivation, the tool
  manifest (`tools.yaml` + `categories.yaml`), update automation, own CI.
  Independently consumable on any NixOS host.
- `kailash-os` — the OS: root flake, the category module tree, profiles,
  images, the `kailash` CLI, tests, release engineering.
- `kailash-website` — this site: generated docs and governance pages, built
  from a pinned manifest revision.

One manifest drives **six system views**: overlay, module tree, desktop menu,
CLI, docs, and the verification evidence matrix. No two surfaces drift. Every
category is an opt-in NixOS module
(`kailash.layers.<layer>.categories.<id>`), generated from the manifest,
VM-tested, never hand-maintained.

Releases are lockfile states: the lockfile is the version. Releases tag
`2026.01-alpha.1` first (staged cuts); bare `2026.01` stays reserved for GA.
The two-digit release index counts releases within the year (01, 02, …,
2026.10, …). Nixpkgs inputs refresh monthly. Tool updates arrive as reviewed
PRs by staleness class. A release train departs every 6 weeks with its images,
checksums, and signed changelog.

## The lab thesis

The platform and the attack tooling ship together. OPS deploys MLflow, vLLM,
TorchServe, vector stores, and agent runtimes as documented lab
configurations. ATTACK carries the platform-exploitation probes validated
against those same deployments. Builders learn to break; breakers learn to
build. One pinned environment carries the distribution's own verification
harness.

## Verification standards

Assurance work binds to the OWASP stack: ASVS 5.0, AISVS 1.0, MLSVS / ML Top
10, and both epochs of the OWASP LLM Top 10 (2026 and v2-2025). Each standard
chapter points to the tools and data packs that test it. `kailash verifier`
records the chapter-by-chapter evidence matrix
([KA-35](https://github.com/kailash-os/kailash-os/issues/35)); the claim
"verified against the standard" then names a runnable command.

## Governance

Kailash ships offensive AI-security tooling for **authorised security work
only** — red-team engagements with written authorisation, academic research,
and defender validation of one's own systems. Users stay responsible for the
law in their jurisdiction (in Australia: Cyber Security Act 2024 (Cth);
Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth), Div 474).

Safety is part of the OS rather than documentation beside it. `KAILASH_LAB_MODE`
defaults off. The OS double-gates active-exploit tooling behind explicit host
and shell opt-in: the host key `kailash.labMode = true` plus the shell key
`KAILASH_LAB_MODE=1` per invocation. No service auto-starts. sops-nix protects
the secrets, and the system reads them at runtime.

## Roadmap

The first release train ran: **[2026.01-alpha.1](https://github.com/kailash-os/kailash-os/releases/tag/2026.01-alpha.1)**
published on 13 October 2026. The tag carries the full four-layer catalogue on
a pinned NixOS base; the generated [Tools page](tools.html) states the census
at each pin. Every release artefact carries SLSA provenance and an SBOM
attestation. The docs estate is live: the
[Kailash OS Guide](https://docs.kailash.tools) and the
[Kailash OS Cookbook](https://book.kailash.tools).

The [Roadmap](roadmap.html) page carries the project timeline and the
release-train plan: every item with its tracking issue and evidence. The
[Kailash Roadmap project board](https://github.com/orgs/kailash-os/projects/1)
carries the work as issues `KA-NN` in
[`kailash-os/kailash-os`](https://github.com/kailash-os/kailash-os). The
[dependency graph](https://github.com/kailash-os/kailash-os/issues/61) is the
canon map.

## Documentation {#documentation}

The docs estate is three sites:

- [kailash.site](https://kailash.site) — project home, paper, and roadmap (this site)
- [docs.kailash.tools](https://docs.kailash.tools) — the user and administrator guide, with a man-style reference page for every tool in the catalogue
- [book.kailash.tools](https://book.kailash.tools) — the cookbook: task-oriented recipes in the Problem → Solution → Discussion → See-also format

The guide explains what a tool is; the cookbook shows how to use it.

## Paper

The paper *"Kailash OS — An Operating System for Building and Securing AI"*
records the design. It carries the taxonomy derivation from MITRE ATLAS and
the OWASP standards, the manifest-driven architecture, the release
engineering of a reproducible OS, and the explicit scope exclusions.

**Read the current revision: [paper.pdf](paper.pdf)** (Revision 1.3, 9 October 2026
— updated as the implementation progresses; the live copy reflects the latest
revision).

The implementation specification carries the phase gates, the packaging
shapes, the manifest schema, and the verification bindings. It is
[`docs/spec.md`](https://github.com/kailash-os/kailash-os/blob/master/docs/spec.md)
in the [project repository](https://github.com/kailash-os/kailash-os).

## Get involved

Kailash is open source under **BSD-3-Clause**. Bundled tools keep their
upstream licences. The packaging harness, the taxonomy, and the CLI accept
contributors: add a tool via a manifest entry, not via hand-edited module
files. CI validates, builds, and tests every change. Sign every commit. Open
an issue on the
[roadmap board](https://github.com/orgs/kailash-os/projects/1), or pick up a
2026.01 train item.
